title: Billy Joel reveals he got brain surgery because he didn’t want to lose his ‘marbles’
text:
Long Island troubadour Billy Joel revealed Tuesday that he underwent brain surgery because he didn’t want to lose his “marbles.”
Speaking on his SiriusXM channel, the 77-year-old “Piano Man” singer admitted he initially balked at going under the knife for hydrocephalus, a disorder he was diagnosed with in 2025.
“I said, ‘Well, what does that entail?’” he said he asked the doctor.
After being told that it involved having a surgeon “drill a hole through your skull” and “stick a shunt inside your brain,” Joel said “I didn’t want to do that.”
“But then I read up on it, and I realized it can help improve your balance and can help your memory,” he said. “You know, I don’t want to lose my marbles. It’s hard to tell what’s age and what’s a condition, so I agreed to do the shunt, and I had surgery, and they implanted a shunt in my brain, and it actually improved things.”
Joel did not say exactly when he had the surgery. But he was diagnosed in May 2025 with normal pressure hydrocephalus, which is a condition in which cerebrospinal fluid builds up inside of the skull and press on the brain, according to the Cleveland Clinic. The condition is often treatable and sometimes reversible.
“They used to call it water on the brain,” Joel said on his radio show.
Joel said he went to see the neurologist because he was feeling unsteady.
“I noticed that my balance was not good,” he said. “I had this sense of being on a boat, like this rocking motion. I wasn’t steady on my feet.”
Will he be returning to the stage anytime soon? Joel didn’t say on his show, and his longtime publicist did not immediately respond to an email from NBC News seeking an answer to that question.
“The doctors told me this: because of my job, which is playing rock and roll music very loud, that it was giving me something like a concussion every time I did a show,” he said.
Pounding out songs on the piano, he said, “was causing damage to my brain nerves, and I could be losing more brain cells the more shows I did. I realized that means I shouldn’t be doing this right now. I got to improve.”
So Joel said he’s been going to physical therapy and following his doctors’ advice.
“I’m doing whatever it is they tell me to do because I don’t want to lose it, you know?” he said.
And he expects to make a full recovery.
“I’m not going anywhere,” he said. “I’m here. I’m still here.”

title: Hurricane Lowell leaves trail of destruction across Kauai
text:
POIPU, Hawaii — On Kauai’s south shore, Hurricane Lowell lifted a home off its foundation and split it in two, the storm’s powerful winds thrusting part of the structure across the street.
At a nearby Sheraton hotel, the hurricane carried several cars across the parking lot and destroyed the hotel’s oceanfront restaurant. Its pool sits full of sand.
These are just two of the many scenes of destruction the hurricane has left in Hawaii after lashing the state’s western islands with heavy rain, widespread flooding and tropical-storm-force winds on Monday and Tuesday.
Now the extensive recovery efforts begin.
Lowell passed just west of the islands of Niihau and Kauai on Monday as a Category 2 hurricane, prompting the National Weather Service to issue the state’s first-ever tornado watch.
Flash flooding was widespread across Kauai, where the NWS recorded preliminary rainfall totals of up to 21 inches.
Kauai County officials said Wednesday that a 74-year-old man had died, most likely because of storm surge generated by Hurricane Lowell, though an investigation is ongoing. One person also died on Oahu, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said, though it has not yet been confirmed that the death was storm-related.
In a video update Wednesday, Kauai County Mayor Derek Kawakami said crews had been dispatched islandwide to assess the aftermath of the storm.
“Plan to be without power for a while,” county officials wrote Wednesday on Facebook. “Some areas should expect several days or longer.”
Around 80% of homes and businesses remain without power in Kauai County — more than 30,000 customers — according to the tracker poweroutage.us.
Gentry Cruz, who manages the property that the storm split in half, was resigned while surveying the extent of the destruction.
“It sucks, but I mean, you cannot do nothing about it,” he said. “Mother Nature is Mother Nature.”
In Waimea, on Kauai’s southwest coast, Facebook user Benjamin E.J. Apilado shared footage of the destruction in his neighborhood early Tuesday, showing fallen coconut trees, downed power lines and an uprooted mango tree that had narrowly missed his car. Other social media users posted videos of destroyed homes, with smashed windows and possessions strewn about. Drone footage captured by photographer Braden Geddes revealed extensive damage to homes and roads across Kauai.
Other islands were also battered, including Oahu, where maximum wind gusts topped 50 mph. Parts of the island were inundated with nearly 10 inches of rain, according to preliminary totals from the NWS.
Lowell has since weakened to a tropical storm and continues to move away from Hawaii, but residual tropical moisture could bring additional precipitation and storms Wednesday over the island chain, which could slow cleanup efforts in some hard-hit areas.
This was far from the first storm to leave a trail of damage in Hawaii over the last six months. Parts of Oahu and the Big Island saw intense flooding from Hurricane Lala just weeks ago, with some additional rain from Tropical Storm Moke on the Big Island soon after. In March, more than 25 inches of rain fell over parts of Oahu, with Maui recording more than 19 inches.
Lowell was one of three storms in the Pacific Ocean last week. The remnants of Hurricane Marie fueled dangerous surf conditions Tuesday along the coast of Southern California, and leftover tropical moisture is driving up temperatures and humidity across the region this week. A rare extreme heat warning was in effect for Southern California on Wednesday, including for Los Angeles and San Diego.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Karina, which had been churning east of the Hawaiian Islands, weakened into a tropical storm on Saturday and did not generate any hazards that affected land.
The uptick in storm activity in the Pacific basin is largely being driven by El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and other forecasting agencies predict an exceptionally strong El Niño, or “super El Niño,” this time around. NOAA last month estimated that this El Niño event has a 69% chance of becoming the strongest on record.

title: Hawaii’s western islands hit by fierce wind from Hurricane Lowell
text:
HONOLULU — Damaging wind and heavy rain from Hurricane Lowell pelted Hawaii’s western islands Tuesday, knocking out power to thousands and ripping up stretches of beachside roads.
Along the Southern California coast, dangerous surf conditions kicked up by the remnants of Hurricane Marie were expected to stick around for several days.
In Hawaii, fierce wind downed trees and caused widespread power outages on the island of Kauai, home to 73,000 residents. The Kauai Island Utility Cooperative reported that nearly all of its roughly 35,000 members were without power early Tuesday.
Emergency officials asked residents to conserve water and stay off the roads as authorities assessed the damage.
Waves that crashed onto Kauai’s southern coast tore apart a road along the coast and pushed piles of sand and lava rocks into a beachside park, said Rochelle Ballard, a former professional surfer who runs a surf school across from the park.
It will take weeks of cleanup, she said. Her family’s surf shop and neighboring restaurant came away without damage, but she said a friend’s house was destroyed.
“It’s going to take a while. I think we’ll be fine,” Ballard said. “We’ve been through this before.”
Hurricane Lowell didn’t make a direct hit on Hawaii
The center of the storm passed west of the islands in the overnight hours Tuesday and moved farther away throughout the day.
The storm’s tropical-storm-force winds extended well beyond the center, the National Hurricane Center said. On Kauai, sustained winds measured just above 50 mph at Lihue Airport, the island’s only commercial airport, which was closed after the storm.
Hurricane warnings for Kauai and the tiny island of Niihau, which has less than 100 permanent residents, were no longer in place by Tuesday morning local time. A tropical storm warning was also lifted for Oahu, the state’s most populated island with close to 1 million residents.
Hurricane Lowell brings heavy rain, strong winds to Hawaii
But flooding and mudslides will continue to be a risk through the day, said Eric Blake of the National Hurricane Center.
Some wind gusts reached 80 mph, according to the hurricane center. But the force of the sustained winds had decreased by early Tuesday and later the storm weakened and was no longer a hurricane. Lowell is expected to continue weakening in the coming days.
Storm left a mess on Kauai and Oahu
There was extensive damage across Kauai, and crews were using heavy equipment to push trees and debris off the roads, said Derek Kawakami, mayor of Kauai County. About 300 people were staying in shelters on Kauai.
Kauai real estate agent Lori Benkert, who lives in Lihue, said she endured a loud, windy night after her power went out Monday evening. The storm downed trees next to her house, and the community’s main road was closed because of fallen trees, she said.
“We’re fine. My house did great with no boarded-up windows,” Benkert said. “But there are a lot of downed power lines.”
On Oahu, road crews were clearing sand and rocks from a major route along the island’s western edge after floodwaters topped a coastal highway, north of Honolulu.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green closed schools and government offices on the three islands for Tuesday ahead of the storm.
Rainfall totals could reach up to 24 inches in some areas on Kauai. Oahu, Maui and the Big Island also could see large amounts of rain.
Last month, Tropical Storm Lala brushed past Hawaii and stirred up landslides, washing away about 100 homes and causing widespread power outages.
Marie downgraded but still being felt in California
What’s left of Hurricane Marie was downgraded again and is no longer considered a tropical storm.
But it was still creating dangerous surf conditions along the coast of Mexico’s Baja California and Southern California. Swells with life-threatening surf and rip current conditions will continue for the next few days, the hurricane center said.
In Malibu, where big waves were pounding the shore, the driveway of a beachfront home that sits on pylons collapsed into a sinkhole Tuesday morning, the Los Angeles County Fire Department said.

title: Hawaii’s western islands hit by fierce winds from Hurricane Lowell, knocking out power
text:
HONOLULU — Damaging wind and heavy rain from Hurricane Lowell pelted Hawaii’s western islands early Tuesday, knocking out power and bringing the threat of flash floods and mudslides.
Along the Southern California coast, dangerous surf conditions kicked up by the remnants of Hurricane Marie were expected to stick around for several days.
In Hawaii, fierce wind downed trees and caused widespread power outages on the island of Kauai, home to 73,000 residents. The Kauai Island Utility Cooperative reported that nearly all of its members were without power early Tuesday.
Emergency officials asked residents to stay off the roads as damage assessments were just beginning.
“As the light comes up and the extent of the damage from Hurricane Lowell comes into focus, we want to ensure that no additional emergency situations arise unnecessarily,” said Elton Ushio, administrator of the local emergency management agency.
The center of the storm passed west of the islands early Tuesday and was moving away, but tropical storm-force wind extended well beyond, the National Hurricane Center said. On Kauai, sustained winds measured just above 50 mph at Lihue Airport.
Hurricane warnings for Kauai and the tiny island of Niihau, which has less than 100 permanent residents, were no longer in place by Tuesday morning local time. A tropical storm warning was also lifted for Oahu, the state’s most populated island with close to 1 million residents.
But flooding and mudslides will continue to be a risk through the day, said Eric Blake, of the National Hurricane Center.
Some wind gusts reached 80 mph, according to the hurricane center. But the force of the sustained wind had decreased by early Tuesday, and the storm was expected to weaken in the coming days.
Road crews were clearing sand and rocks from a major route along Oahu’s western edge after floodwaters topped a coastal highway, north of Honolulu.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green closed schools and government offices on the three islands for Tuesday ahead of the storm.
Rainfall totals could reach up to 24 inches in some areas on Kauai. Oahu, Maui and the Big Island also could see large amounts of rain.
Last month, Tropical Storm Lala brushed past Hawaii and stirred up landslides, washing away about 100 homes and causing widespread power outages.

title: Nepal holds a day of mourning after floods kill at least 1,300 people
text:
KATHMANDU, Nepal — Nepal held a day of mourning Monday to remember those killed in the Aug. 26 floods, with flags lowered at government offices and families concluding mourning rituals.
Monday was the 13th day since the flooding, which killed more than 1,300 people in Nepal and Tibet and left some 5,000 missing, including foreigners, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.
In predominantly Hindu Nepal, mourning periods last 13 days, during which close family members stay home and relatives visit to pay their respects. Rituals are held on the final day to pray for the souls of the departed.
Several people whose relatives remain missing performed symbolic funerals. Cremation is an important final rite in Hindu tradition, and performing the ceremony even without the bodies of their loved ones provided some families a sense of spiritual release.
The government had declared Monday an official day of mourning and ordered flags at government offices lowered to half-staff.
Meanwhile, search efforts continued for the missing, but some protested that not enough was being done.
In Kathmandu, relatives gathered near the offices of the prime minister and key ministries to demand the government speed up search and rescue efforts for hundreds of people who had been working at hydropower plants and were either swept away by the rushing Bhotekhoshi River or buried under debris.
Sumana Shrestha stood with family members holding a poster with the photo of her 55-year-old husband, who has not been heard from since the day of the flood.
Her husband, a consulting geologist, had promised to return home after his shift at the project office for the Trishuli hydropower plant on the day of the flood. The 2 1/2-story office was completely buried by debris.
“We are here because we have not heard of any rescue attempt on this project, but it has been 13 days already,” she said. “The only thing we have been able to do is pray to God and hope for a miracle.”
Another protester, Mahesh Prasad Shrestha, held a photograph of his brother Niraj Shrestha, a 52-year-old engineer who worked at the same site. He said authorities only sent a small excavator by helicopter on the sixth or seventh day after the disaster, adding: “They should have ordered big helicopters from places like China or India to fly in equipment.”
Candlelight vigils were held in several places in Kathmandu in memory of the people who lost their lives during the flooding.
Rescue efforts have focused on 12 hydropower projects, where about 900 workers are missing and roughly 500 are believed to be trapped in various tunnels, authorities said. Specialized rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the United States have been searching through debris, damaged structures and tunnels at the projects.
Two Nepalese workers were rescued from the plant Friday, and rescuers pulled out a Chinese man from the facility on Saturday.

title: Hurricane Lowell brings 30-foot surf as it nears western Hawaiian islands
text:
One of Hawaii’s westernmost main islands was hit with damaging surf of 30 feet and offshore winds of over 100 mph as Category 2 Hurricane Lowell approached Monday, officials said.
The hurricane, with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph, posed a risk to all the major islands due to the possibility of heavy rains and landslides, forecasters warned.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said in a 5 p.m. local time update that there have been winds of around 100 mph and greater offshore of Kauai.
“They’re having a huge impact, 20- to 30-foot surf, damaging a lot of the area right around the shoreline,” he said in a video posted to social media.
Kauai County, which includes the islands of Kauai, Niʻihau, Lehua, and Kaʻula, was under a hurricane warning, the National Hurricane Center said.
Lowell is expected to pass to the west of Kauai and Niʻihau late Monday and early Tuesday morning, the agency said. Oahu was under a tropical storm warning.
Kauai County Mayor Derek Kawakami urged residents to be off the roads by midday on Monday. He credited the Kauai emergency management team whose preparations put the county “in a good position to be able to weather this storm as one community.”
“Hurricane Lowell is going to come a little closer than anticipated, and what that really means to everybody is that we are asking everyone to start sheltering in place,” Kawakami said.
Residents who live in flood zones were advised to call friends and family members in safer areas to see if they would be able to house them. Officials referred people to refuge centers as a last resort.
“I have to say, what I’ve observed over the last few days is nothing less than phenomenal,” Kawakami said. “I’ve seen people getting out there, getting prepared.”
The island of Niʻihau, located less than 20 miles southwest of Kauai, does not have a mayor and is technically part of Kauai County.
The worst of the storm is expected to occur overnight, but that could change, according to Kauai Emergency Management Administrator Elton Ushio. He warned of a threat of wind, water, flooding and storm surge.
“Conditions are rapidly deteriorating,” Ushio said. “You know we’re having multiple rivers reaching flood stage. ... We could have a prolonged closure out there of the Kuhio Highway, but other areas island-wide could be affected.”
Hurricane Lowell’s maximum sustained winds were 110 mph at around 5 p.m. local time Monday (10 p.m. ET), the National Hurricane Center said.
The storm is expected to weaken over the next several days. “However, Lowell is forecast to remain a hurricane as it passes near the Hawaiian Islands,” the agency said.
The core of the storm is forecast to move near or just west of Niʻihau Monday night or Tuesday, it said.
Storm surges of 2 to 4 feet are expected, as well as up to 16 inches of rain. The wet conditions on the island’s hills and mountains increase the risk of flash flooding and mudslides.
There is also a possibility that the islands could see tornadoes form due to the high winds.
Lowell previously reached Category 5 status but has since weakened. It’s the one of three cyclones that have swirled in the Pacific over the last week; the others are Hurricane Karina and Hurricane Marie, which brought rain and high surf to Southern California.
This high level of storm activity in the Pacific is consistent with expectations for El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean. This year’s El Niño is forecast to be exceptionally intense, possibly record-breaking.
Hawaii is still recovering from previous bouts of heavy rain and flooding after Tropical Storm Lala impacted the Big Island last month. At least one person died in a storm-related car crash and more than 100,000 people lost power.
Just a week later, Tropical Storm Moke brought more rain. Now, as Lowell passes, some areas of Big Island could once again see up to 12 inches of rain, potentially compounding the prior storms’ effects.
All flights were canceled Monday for Lihue Airport, Kauai’s only airport, due to the hurricane, the state Department of Transportation said. There will be inspections of runways and facilities before they resume, it added.
The Kauai Emergency Management Agency urged residents to fill gas tanks, charge devices, refill prescriptions and gather water and food ahead of the storm. Residents should be prepared to stay home for several days, the agency said.
The county’s department of water similarly recommended that residents stock up on drinking water and fill buckets and bathtubs for nondrinking use.
Green announced that state and county offices in Kauai, including public schools, would be closed until Tuesday due to concerns about Lowell. He urged residents to follow guidance from local officials and remain indoors.
“Closing offices, schools and courts will help keep people off the roads during dangerous conditions and allow emergency crews to focus on protecting our communities,” Green said.
Residents began preparations as early as Wednesday, a manager of Kauai’s only Home Depot told NBC News affiliate KHNL. The station reported that the store was bought of out generators, tarps, and other emergency gear.
Resident Nouveau Naumu told KHNL that he was 10 years old when Hawaii was hit by Hurricane Iniki. He remembered the devastation the 1992 storm left and was not taking Lowell lightly, he said.
“I just remember the high winds, us kind of huddling in the bathroom and things were just hitting the house, all the debris, and then waking up the next morning you could see the devastation,” Naumu said.

title: Hurricane Lowell menaces Hawaiian Islands with life-threatening surf
text:
Hurricane Lowell is expected to create life-threatening conditions even as it is forecast to pass just west of the major Hawaiian islands by Monday night.
It could remain a major hurricane — those with 111 mph or greater sustained winds — and is likely to create mudslides, as much as 10 inches of rain in Kauai, and life-threatening waves for parts of the island chain, the National Hurricane Center said.
Lowell turned north Sunday, as a hurricane warning for the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument was issued. By Sunday evening, Kauai County, which covers the islands of Kauai and Niʻihau, was placed under a hurricane watch.
Lowell was about 500 miles south-southwest of the community of Līhuʻe, on the westernmost major Hawaiian island of Kauai, according to the hurricane center’s Sunday evening advisory, and was moving at 9 mph.
The tropical cyclone reached Category 5, defined by sustained winds of 157 mph or greater, overnight Friday before losing some of its steam and settling into Category 4’s limits of sustained winds of 130-156 mph by Saturday. On Sunday, its 120 mph sustained winds placed it in Category 3.
The hurricane center’s forecast cone has Lowell passing just west of the archipelago’s major islands, from south to north, on Monday night.
“Just because we’re on the edge of the cone doesn’t mean we’re safe,” John Bravender, warning coordination meteorologist at the National Weather Service, said at a Friday news conference.
Maui could record up to 8 inches of rain, the National Hurricane Center said, but officials in the state are also focused on the storm’s impacts on Kauai and Niʻihau, the latter occupying the map as the archipelago’s 84-resident, westernmost island.
“Hurricane Lowell has made its expected northward turn and remains forecast to pass west of Kauaʻi, but a slight shift east has increased the potential for tropical storm-force winds,” Gov. Josh Green said Sunday on X. “The greatest impacts are expected Monday, particularly on Kauaʻi and Niʻihau.”
The state’s Emergency Management Agency said Sunday that tropical storm conditions were expected in Kauai County in the next 36 hours, while Ni‘ihau, Kauai and the surfing mecca of Oahu could see “extremely dangerous surf” on south- and west-facing coastlines Monday and Tuesday.
Niʻihau and Kauaʻi could see 12 to 14 inches of rain, it said, with downpours expected to begin Sunday afternoon and flash flooding and landslides possible.
On Friday, Green declared a state of emergency for Hawaii and activated the National Guard to respond to the storm’s impacts.
“We are taking Hurricane Lowell extremely seriously and preparing now, before conditions deteriorate,” Green said in a statement Friday. “I urge everyone, especially those in Kauaʻi County, to complete their preparations, follow official alerts and stay away from floodwaters, dangerous surf and other hazardous areas.”
The governor’s office said the state was securing its harbors, deploying emergency personnel to strategic locations and monitoring dams for any possible breaches or overflows.
Parts of Oahu and the Big Island were hit with intense flooding and strong winds from Tropical Storm Lala last month.
Lowell is joined by two other tropical cyclones spinning in the northern half of the Pacific this week: Tropical Storm Karina, a former Category 4 hurricane about 655 miles east-northeast of Hilo, Hawaii, on Sunday; and Hurricane Marie, churning about 550 miles west-southwest of Punta Eugenia, Mexico, and producing 75 mph sustained winds — a hair above the threshold for Category 1 status.
Marie is producing high surf that could bring life-threatening waves and rip currents to some Southern California locations during the holiday weekend, hurricane center meteorologists said Sunday.
The trio is part of a northeast Pacific hurricane season that includes 15 named storms to date, according to Colorado State University. The high number is likely boosted by unusually warm water and the presence of an El Niño weather phenomenon that could also bring historic rain to California, experts have said.
Daniel Gilford, a meteorologist and atmospheric scientist at the nonprofit research group Climate Central, said El Niño’s warm sea surface temperatures are fueling potent tropical cyclones ahead of fall.
“If we have extra fuel, we can push the accelerator down more and these storms can become more intense as a result,” he told NBC News.
The phenomenon has been changing as a result of global warming, earth scientists have said, with United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres saying Thursday that El Niño is “being supersized before our eyes.”
It’s a call to action to address climate change, he said.

title: Three hurricanes churn in the Pacific, one that could affect Hawaii, as El Niño ramps up
text:
Three hurricanes — Karina, Lowell and Marie — are churning in the Pacific Ocean, a high level of activity that climate scientists say is on brand for El Niño, especially given that this year’s event is likely to become the strongest on record.
Two of the storms hit major hurricane status this week. Lowell, which could target Hawaii this weekend, reached Category 5 strength Wednesday and has since weakened to Category 3. The storm is moving west but expected to make a sharp turn to the north over the weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center, taking it near the islands of Oahu and Kauai.
The forecast comes as Hawaii is still recovering from multiple instances of heavy rain and flash flooding over the last six months. Just weeks ago, parts of Oahu and the Big Island were hit with intense flooding and strong winds from Tropical Storm Lala. Damage also remains from devastating floods in March, when more than 25 inches of rain fell in some parts of Oahu and more than 19 inches in parts of Maui.
Meanwhile, Karina has weakened from Category 3 to Category 2 east of the Hawaiian Islands and is forecast to weaken further over the next 48 hours, according to the hurricane center. Marie, located nearly 400 miles off the coast of Mexico’s Baja California Peninsula, is strengthening. The storm could generate strong swells for portions of Mexico’s southwestern coast and Baja California through the weekend, and perhaps Southern California, too, according to the hurricane center.
The trio of hurricanes represents a level of elevated activity consistent with El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean.
This year, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and other forecasting agencies predict an exceptionally strong El Niño, or “super El Niño,” marked by water temperatures at least 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above average in the Pacific.
NOAA’s forecast last month suggested that this El Niño event has a 69% chance of becoming the strongest on record.
El Niño typically exacerbates warming from human-caused climate change, further boosting global temperatures and increasing the likelihood of extreme weather.
In El Niño years, the high sea surface temperatures help more Pacific storms to form and grow. Daniel Gilford, a meteorologist and atmospheric scientist at the nonprofit research group Climate Central, likened tropical cyclones to a car engine, with warm ocean water acting like fuel.
“The engine needs some sort of fuel to convert into wind,” he said. “If we increase the amount of fuel available to a storm, it’s kind of like increasing the speed limit on your car. If we have extra fuel, we can push the accelerator down more and these storms can become more intense as a result.”
This El Niño event has taken hold at a time when sea surface temperatures in the Pacific were already significantly elevated. Scientists have been tracking a vast marine heat wave — a prolonged period of unusually high ocean temperatures — in the Pacific that began last year. Gilford said that Climate Central’s early studies have found that about 94% of the Pacific has experienced heat wave conditions since January, with some regions already up to 2 degrees Celsius warmer than normal.
“Temperatures across the entire Pacific Ocean are elevated, and we’re certainly seeing that in the region where these hurricanes and tropical cyclones are traversing,” he said.
In contrast to the flurry of activity in the Pacific, things are relatively quiet in the Atlantic basin — yet another characteristic of El Niño, according to Gilford.
“El Niño conditions change the winds in the atmosphere in such a way that they are not conducive to storms forming in the Atlantic Ocean,” he said. “That’s exactly what we’re seeing right now.”
Although El Niño is a natural pattern, climate scientists think it may be intensifying as a result of climate change. A study in the journal Science last month found that El Niño events have strengthened since humans started burning fossil fuels that send heat-trapping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.
United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Thursday that El Niño is “being supersized before our eyes,” a situation that should be a call to action.
“The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up,” Guterres said in response to a new World Meteorological Organization report on the strengthening El Niño. “Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”

title: Two trapped workers are pulled alive from Nepal tunnel more than a week after deadly floods
text:
POKHARA, Nepal — Two workers in Nepal were pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after devastating floods swept the Himalayan region and left thousands of people dead or missing.
In a rare glimmer of hope, emergency teams rescued two men — a mechanical foreman named Sanjay Sah, 30, and a mechanical supervisor named Kabir Maharjan, 45, according to Nepal’s army and the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority. A body was also recovered, Nepal’s army said.
Two Nepal flood survivors rescued from hydropower tunnel
Rescue officials said the voices of other workers could be heard inside the tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s border district of Rasuwa. At least 557 workers are still believed to be missing there, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
In a video shared by Nepalese authorities, Sah said he spent his days trapped underground “chanting mantras to give myself hope” while hearing others trapped and calling out for help.
Sah said the “primary duty” of his job is “to safeguard everyone’s life,” adding that there were some 40 to 50 people in the tunnel at the time of the incident.
“I made sure to evacuate everyone else, but I didn’t get the chance to escape myself,” he said, speaking from the hospital in the video.
He said there could still be other survivors on his side of the tunnel, while there could be workers on the powerhouse side of the tunnel “who didn’t make it out in time.”
Nepal’s army released images of the dramatic rescue on its official Facebook page, including one showing the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
“When hope is alive, even the impossible becomes possible,” the image caption read.
Officials said both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, the capital, for treatment.
“I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God,” Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.
The large-scale operation has involved 75 army personnel, 18 police officers and multiple experts, the army said.
Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said one of the survivors told rescuers that more people were still alive inside the tunnel.
“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.
More than 900 workers are missing from about a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local officials.
Rescuers have been struggling to access the hydropower projects, many of which are in remote, mountainous areas, with bad weather adding to the difficulties. The flooding damaged roads and collapsed sections of tunnels, filling them with mud and other debris and blocking some entrances.
Aided by foreign experts, rescue teams have been working around the clock using controlled blasts, excavators and earth-moving equipment to try to reach the trapped workers amid concerns about air quality in the tunnels and the workers’ access to drinking water.
Nepal’s army said Friday that a separate rescue effort had recovered two bodies from a tunnel at the Langtang Hydropower Project.
Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,294 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after the Aug. 26 disaster, which is believed to have been set off by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region.
Nepal’s disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.
Nepalese authorities said a national day of mourning will be observed on Sept. 7 in honor of those who lost their lives during the flood. The national flag will be flown at half-staff at government offices and Nepali embassies and missions abroad.
Rescue efforts are also still underway in China, where a mudslide hit a major land crossing between the two countries, with the only road to the site in Tibet’s Gyirong county fully reopening only Wednesday. Chinese officials say at least 31 people were killed and 531 are missing on the Tibet side of the border.
More than 800 foreign nationals are among those missing in the area, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. According to the State Department, 75 Americans remained unaccounted for as of Wednesday, while 16 had made their way to safety.
Sunil Pandey reported from Pokhara, Nepal, and Adela Suliman from London.

title: Former Tropical Storm Edouard lingers over Texas, flooding homes and roads
text:
LIVINGSTON, Texas — Texas authorities rescued dozens of people from stranded cars, homes surrounded by floodwaters and an assisted living facility Wednesday as former Tropical Storm Edouard lingered over rural parts of the state and dumped nearly 2 feet of rain in some places.
Heavy rains from the storm, which weakened into a tropical depression after making landfall Tuesday, were expected to threaten the eastern part of the state through Thursday morning, the National Weather Service said.
Meanwhile, a burst of tropical weather persisted in the Pacific Ocean, where three hurricanes were churning in open waters.
In Texas’ hard-hit Hardin County, about 85 miles northeast of Houston, flooding, downed trees and power lines, debris, and power outages were still creating hazardous conditions, officials said.
Between 18 inches and 20 inches fell in parts of the county over the last two days, the weather service said. The average local monthly rainfall for September is just 5.51 inches, said Nick Slaughter, a meteorologist with the weather service.
Across the area close to the Louisiana border, schools and municipal offices were closed, and residents were told to stay home.
Edouard downs trees, floods roads and leaves drivers stranded
Hardin County’s office of emergency management said Wednesday afternoon that 12 motorists had to be rescued after driving into flooded roadways, two people had to be rescued from a flooded home, about 10 structures were damaged by trees and thousands were still without power.
In Jefferson County, located about 80 miles northeast of Houston, the main concern was restoring power after trees and limbs were brought down during the storm, which had wind gusts up to 90 mph, said Robert Grimm, the county emergency management coordinator. About 22,000 customers in the county were without power as of late Wednesday afternoon, nearly half of the 50,000 utility customers affected statewide, according to poweroutage.com.
Grady Leger said that as the storm moved through Hardin County on Tuesday evening, a power line went down by his home near Lumberton, and he could feel the vibration coming up from the ground.
“Some blue and yellow, white sparks caught part of my dead tree on fire,” Leger said.
An assisted living facility was damaged in Hardin County, and 21 people were evacuated, according to Texas Parks and Wildlife, whose game wardens assisted. Photos from the agency showed some officials wading in thigh-deep water in parts of the county.
Edouard is expected to dissipate Thursday.
3 hurricanes are in the Pacific Ocean
Hurricane Marie strengthened from a tropical storm on Wednesday well offshore of southwest Mexico in the Pacific, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said.
Swells generated by the storm were expected to affect parts of coastal southwestern Mexico and the Baja California peninsula over the next few days. They will likely spread to Southern California over the weekend, the center said.
Hurricane Lowell, a Category 4 storm, was hundreds of miles south of Hawaii on Wednesday. It briefly strengthened to a Category 5 storm before weakening again, and it was expected to remain powerful over the next several days. Swells generated by Lowell are likely to affect parts of the Hawaiian Islands beginning Wednesday, the center said.
Regarding Marie and Lowell, swells “are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions,” the center said.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hurricane Karina strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm. Forecasters said it should weaken over the next few days.

images.caption: Flooding near Honey Island, Texas, after Tropical Storm Edouard, on Wednesday. Brett Coomer / Houston Chronicle via AP
Satellite imagery captured Wednesday shows three storms in the Pacific Ocean: from left, Hurricane Lowell, Hurricane Karina and Tropical Storm Marie. CIRA / NOAA via AP

title: Rep. David Schweikert describes surviving deadly Grand Canyon flash flood
text:
Rep. David Schweikert, R-Ariz., said he heard what sounded like “a freight train smashing into a boulder” as a Grand Canyon flash flood consumed the landscape near his rafting group Saturday.
Schweikert told NBC News from his office in Washington on Tuesday that the loud crash was followed by a powerful stream of mud and debris-filled water.
Two visitors died and another is still missing after flash flooding from a sudden deluge of rain briefly transformed Bright Angel Creek into a full-fledged river. About 80 people were evacuated from campsites around the historic Phantom Ranch area of the park.
The retiring member of Congress and the rest of his group were about 100 yards away from the danger zone without cellphone service. His guide led the group to an area off the Colorado River near Bright Angel Creek.
They later left the area on foot — traveling on higher ground — and camped for the night nearby.
It is “monsoon season” in Arizona, but Schweikert said there was not more than a drizzle of precipitation where he was when the dangerous flood ripped through, underscoring the potential randomness of such events.
“At some point, you realized this is a big deal; something’s really gone haywire. ... It was a ginormous flash flood,” he said.
The intricate terrain of the Grand Canyon can invite the type of deadly flood conditions that hit the southern part of the national park over the weekend.
“The deluge downpour could have been miles away and was channeled into the canyon, and what used to be a creek now is a river,” said Schweikert, who is a regular Grand Canyon hiker.
The water supply system for the park was also severely damaged, along with part of a new $208 million water pipeline project that was underway near the ranch.
Schweikert said he would likely be involved in working to get the damage addressed once proper assessments are made. “Right now, the heartbreak is a couple of people lost their lives,” he added.
He also cautioned visitors to the park to carefully monitor the weather and to use extreme caution if storms are expected in the vicinity at all. If storms are nearby, hikes through narrow passages known as slot canyons should be strictly avoided because of the risk of getting trapped, the seasoned adventurer said.
“It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Schweikert said.

images.caption: “It’s remarkable beauty, but you always take it seriously because the canyon will sneak up on you if you’re not prepared,” Rep. David Schweikert said. Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

videos.caption: Crews at the Grand Canyon are confronting difficult terrain as they try to find a missing hiker. We’re also seeing new images of flash flooding in Zion National Park. NBC News’ Dana Griffin is in the flood zone.

title: Edouard weakens into a tropical depression after landfall but still dumps rain into Texas
text:
PORT ARTHUR, Texas — The former Tropical Storm Edouard weakened into a depression Tuesday night while unleashing heavy rains and strong winds on parts of Texas, knocking out power to thousands, toppling trees and flooding roads.
The storm was downgraded hours after it made landfall near the Texas-Louisiana border with maximum sustained winds of 60 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center. Forecasters said the system would keep losing strength as it pushed inland but would likely continue to produce heavy rains and possible flooding into Wednesday.
Meanwhile, a burst of tropical weather continued in the Pacific, where three named storms were churning in open waters.
The hurricane center expected Edouard to dump 3 to 7 inches of rain with up to 12 inches in some areas.
Storm makes landfall along Texas-Louisiana line
As the center of the storm passed over Beaumont, Texas, about 80 miles northeast of Houston, the city’s offices were shuttered and the Texas Office of Emergency Management warned residents to stay off the road.
Throughout the city were downed trees blocking roads, traffic signals that weren’t working and flooded underpasses, Beaumont police said on social media.
About 32,000 utility customers were without electricity in Jefferson County, which includes Beaumont, according to poweroutage.com.
Mike Gilbert decided ahead of the storm to close his surf shop on Texas’ Crystal Beach because he didn’t want to risk his employees having a difficult time getting home. But, he said, it had ended up just being gray skies and drizzly rain there Tuesday as Edouard made landfall about 60 miles northeast of his shop.
“You literally never know,” Gilbert said. “It could have all of a sudden moved over 50 miles and picked up 20 mph in wind and it could have been a whole different story.”
In Cameron, Louisiana, the winds had picked up by Tuesday morning, and rain was coming through on and off, said Connor Salvador, who owns an RV park there near the coast. He said while there could be a “little bit” of flooding if they get a lot of rain, he wasn’t too worried about Edouard.
“We’re pretty used to all these types of storms that come through,” he said.
Several storms in the Pacific Ocean
Forecasters said newly formed Hurricane Lowell in the Pacific Ocean was expected to remain several hundred miles away from Hawaii for the next several days at least, but swells from the hurricane were likely to affect parts of the islands beginning Wednesday.
“This hurricane is likely to increase the surf and make for dangerous beach conditions and marine conditions for any boaters near the Hawaiian Islands over the next few days,” said Andrew Hagan, a forecaster with the National Hurricane Center.
Tropical Storm Marie formed in the Pacific Ocean early Tuesday well offshore of southwest Mexico, the center said. Forecasters said it was expected to become a hurricane by Wednesday night, and swells generated by the storm were expected to affect parts of the coast in southwestern Mexico and the Baja California peninsula over the next few days.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Karina became a hurricane Sunday, fueled by warm waters far from any shore. It strengthened Monday into a powerful Category 4 storm, but forecasters said Tuesday that it was expected to weaken.

images.caption: A medical worker heads to work Tuesday in Beaumont, Texas, during Tropical Storm Edouard. Antranik Tavitian / Getty Images
A storm-damaged G.I. Surplus store in Beaumont. Antranik Tavitian / Getty Images

videos.caption: The remnants of Tropical Storm Edouard are still packing a punch after making landfall along the Texas coast, leaving tens of thousands without power and putting millions in the path of dangerous storms, floods and brutal heat. NBC’s Jesse Kirsch reports and TODAY’s Dylan Dreyer tracks the latest forecast.

title: Karina strengthens into a Category 4 hurricane in the Pacific far from land, forecasters say
text:
MIAMI — Hurricane Karina strengthened Monday into a powerful Category 4 storm in the Pacific Ocean but isn’t threatening land, forecasters said.
The storm has intensified quickly since becoming a hurricane Sunday and has been fueled by warm waters far offshore, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said.
Karina was about 1,020 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico and had maximum sustained winds of 145 mph, the center said. It was moving west.
There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but waves were expected to affect Mexico and likely Southern California. Additional strengthening was possible on Monday, followed by fluctuations in intensity.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Lowell was about 855 miles east-southeast of Hilo, Hawaii. The storm had maximum sustained winds of 60 mph and was moving west.
Forecasters said Lowell could become a hurricane by Monday night or Tuesday. The storm posed no immediate threat to land, but the center said Lowell could be in the vicinity of the Hawaiian Islands later this week.

title: At least 1 dead, more than a dozen missing at Grand Canyon after extreme flash flooding
text:
At least one person is dead and more than a dozen others are missing or unaccounted for, park officials said, after flash floods overwhelmed a remote area of the Grand Canyon Sunday.
Forecasters warned that more flash flooding was possible on Monday. The biggest threat of flash flooding on Monday is set to be just north of the Grand Canyon.
The catastrophic flooding prompted the National Park Service to cancel or bar all overnight stays, and impose water conservation measures.
The National Park Service is asking for information about anyone who may have been hiking or backpacking along Bright Angel Creek in Arizona, as well as campers with plans to stay at Phantom Ranch or the Bright Angel Campground.
Officials are also trying to track down travelers who might have been stranded along the North Kaibab Trail.
The National Park Service said in an evening update that a 46-year-old man was recovered from Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. The Coconino County Medical Examiner’s Office was at the scene, the NPS said.
The flooding is already restricting the visitors’ use of the canyon.
All park concessions will halt overnight accommodations during the peak visitor season and water restrictions on the South Rim will begin as of noon on Monday, the NPS said. There had been “extensive damage” to infrastructure in the inner canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, which supplies water from the canyon for use in the park, it said.
“The waterline is currently not operational, leaving the park with limited water reserves and requiring significant water conservation measures to ensure available supplies can be maintained,” the service said.
The National Weather Service warned that the threat of flash flooding in all of northern and central Arizona remained through Monday evening.
The park service earlier Sunday said 15 people were missing or unaccounted for, down from a previous estimate of 20.
Among those missing is a Texas chiropractor who had been chronicling his trip to the Grand Canyon on Facebook. His sister told the New York Times that they last spoke to him on Saturday afternoon before the flooding began.
As of Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail. Additional evacuations from Phantom Ranch and the Cottonwood Campground were expected.
Park administrators also said that footbridges along Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, “eliminating hiker access across the creek,” and that certain Colorado River crossings were closed while damage is assessed.
“The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon,” the National Park Service said in a statement. “Grand Canyon National Park staff are continuing to assess damage to trails, bridges, utilities, facilities and other infrastructure.”
Phantom Ranch is accessible only by hiking, raft or mule transport. It has been a coveted Grand Canyon destination since it opened in 1922.
Colorado River traffic was also shut down because of the risk of floating debris.
David Gregory was one of many in the area on Sunday. He told NBC News he spent Saturday morning hiking down the North Kaibab Trail to Phantom Ranch and had just checked into a cabin a couple of hours before the rain hit.
Hours later, officials told him and his group they needed to evacuate. After grabbing their things, Gregory said they crossed some footbridges before first responders airlifted him and about 50 others to safety.
“It was kind of crazy hearing later that the bridge that we crossed was wiped out. Kind of makes you think that maybe we should have been in more of a panic,” Gregory said.

images.caption: Heavy flooding in Grand Canyon National Park on Sunday. Craig Sanderson via AP
Remnants of stone bridge pylons remain along Bright Angel Creek following a flash flood that destroyed the footbridge Saturday. Grand Canyon National Park

title: Karina rapidly intensifies into a major hurricane in the Pacific
text:
MIAMI — Hurricane Karina formed Sunday in the Pacific Ocean and swiftly intensified into a dangerous major storm within hours, fueled by warm waters far offshore where it poses no immediate threat to land.
Karina gained Category 1 hurricane status early Sunday with top sustained winds of 80 mph and then took mere hours to jump up to a dangerous Category 3 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 125 mph, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said.
A major hurricane is a Category 3 or greater with maximum sustained winds of at least 111 mph. Meteorologists said some additional strengthening is possible over the next day or so.
On Sunday, Karina was located about 960 miles west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico’s Baja California Peninsula and was moving west at 9 mph. It was on a forecast path expected to take it farther out into the Pacific.
While Karina was expected to stay well away from land, swells from the storm were likely to cause dangerous surf and rip current conditions along stretches of coastline in southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, the hurricane center said. There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
Elsewhere in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Lowell was about 985 miles east-southeast of Hilo, Hawaii. The storm had maximum sustained winds of 50 mph and posed no immediate threat to land. Forecasters said Sunday that Lowell could become a hurricane by Monday night or Tuesday.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast a below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to El Niño.
It predicted eight to 14 named storms, with three to six of them reaching hurricane strength and one to three intensifying to major hurricanes.

images.caption: While Karina was expected to stay well away from land, swells from the storm were likely to cause dangerous surf and rip current conditions along parts of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula, the hurricane center said. NOAA

title: Tropical Storms Karina and Lowell form in the Pacific Ocean as Dolly churns in the Atlantic
text:
MIAMI — Tropical Storms Karina and Lowell formed Thursday in the Pacific Ocean, both of which were expected to become hurricanes in the next few days, the National Hurricane Center said.
Tropical Storm Karina was located about 825 miles (1,330 kilometers) south of the southern tip of Baja California, with maximum sustained winds of around 45 mph (75 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center.
Tropical Storm Lowell was about 1,765 miles (2,840 kilometers) west-southwest of the tip of Baja California, with maximum sustained winds of around 40 mph (65 kph).
There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect for either storm, though the hurricane center warned swells from Karina could bring life-threatening surf and rip currents to portions of southwest Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula over the weekend.
Earlier Thursday, Tropical Storm Dolly formed in the Atlantic Ocean far from land, and forecasters said it could bring heavy rain to portions of the Caribbean.
The storm was about 1,555 miles (2,500 kilometers) east of the Leeward Islands and had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph (64 kph), the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said. Dolly was moving west.
The storm and its name had no connection to Dolly Parton’s death Tuesday.
Storm systems are named by procedures set by the World Meteorological Organization, and the lists of names are reused every six years. For the Atlantic region, the lists are alphabetical and alternate male and female names.
Dolly was the fourth named storm for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.
There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect, but the center said the Leeward Islands could get heavy rain Saturday and Sunday. The Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico and Hispaniola could see heavy rain Sunday and Monday.
Little change in strength is forecast during the coming days, the center said, but flash flooding could occur.
The Atlantic hurricane season started with Tropical Storm Arthur coming ashore on the U.S. Gulf Coast in June, and Tropical Storm Bertha dumped rain in Louisiana and Texas in July. Tropical Storm Cristobal formed and quickly dissipated in the Atlantic earlier in August.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast a below-average Atlantic hurricane season due to El Nino. It forecast eight to 14 named storms, with three to six of them reaching hurricane strength and one to three of those intensifying to major hurricanes.
The NHC and other weather agencies name storms to easily communicate warnings about them to people and to avoid confusion. The WMO says names are chosen to be short, easy to pronounce and familiar to the regions of the world where the storm names are used. It meets regularly to evaluate potential names, and some names are retired for reasons of sensitivity, particularly for deadly or destructive storms.
One name from the 2025 season was retired, Melissa, which was a Category 5 hurricane that brought devastation to the Caribbean.

images.caption: A satellite image of Tropical Storm Dolly over the Atlantic Ocean on Aug. 27. NOAA via AP
